selections.speaker: Max
selections.text: Would be a fun piece to write and cool to link to some of the games or even host them since some of them run in browser like the old mac and dos games. I also remember my dad getting a macintosh magazine with games on a disc, i think the one pack we got that i played a ton of had a game called chrysanthemum and there was a tank battle thing, maybe turn based. there was also another one that was like rogue pixel dungeon but super old school. and there was a sort of galaga clone with insects.

selections.speaker: Claude
selections.text:
**The turn-based tank battle** — unresolved. The iconic Mac tank game is **Bolo**, but it's real-time networked multiplayer, not turn-based. Either the memory has drifted or it's something smaller off the same disc. Look at a couple of screenshots and tell me.

[…]

Chrysanthemum plus Swoop on one disc points at a mid-90s Mac shareware compilation rather than a magazine's own disc, so the disc itself is probably findable too.

selections.text: The MacAddict discs are raw HFS images, but the HFS catalog stores filenames in plaintext — so I can read the partition map and catalog extents over HTTP range requests and search a 650 MB disc by pulling about a megabyte of it. Building that.

selections.speaker: Claude
selections.text:
Two things that would narrow this a lot faster than brute force:

[…]

**Was the Mac color or black-and-white?** Chrysanthemum ran on System 7.0 through 7.6, and TaskMaker had a B&W 1989 release and a color 1993 one. Which version you remember dates the disc.

[…]

**Do you remember the magazine at all** — MacAddict, Macworld, MacUser, Mac Home Journal? MacAddict didn't start until September 1996, so if the disc came home in 1994 it was one of the others and I should re-point the sweep.

selections.speaker: Max
selections.text: I remember black and white. some color apps. i might be conflating since i was like 3-7. that goes for the magazines too.

arcade-architecture.excerpt: emulation and saves run in the browser, while the cluster serves immutable files.
arcade-architecture.context: Selected clause from the completed hosting preparation report. The issue is private; this curated excerpt lets a visitor read the relevant statement without a GitLab account.

detail.note: Selected architecture and test observations from the September 7 preparation comment. This is a work record, with deployment instructions and internal artifact locations omitted.

selections.speaker: Codex
selections.text:
The prepared architecture is `/arcade`, `/arcade/<game>` and two disc pages on probablyfine.dev, embedding **our own** `arcade.probablyfine.dev` runtime. All emulator code, Mac system media, game disks and MacCube CD ranges are local to its static nginx image. Source sites are credited rather than used as visitor media backends. The image serves 12 games, including GTA 2 in a browser-run Windows 95 machine. No per-player server VM or Ceph PVC is required: emulation and saves run in the browser, while the cluster serves immutable files.

[…]

Actual gameplay/interactions and complete CD navigation were checked; Mac folder persistence and the visible DOS save control passed. GTA 2 retained saves, physical joysticks and all browser/mobile combinations remain unverified and are described accordingly.

dns-diagnosis.excerpt: The Ingress routes to a Service named `dummy` that does not exist, in a namespace holding nothing else.
dns-diagnosis.context: Selected sentence from the investigation record. The historical account posted under Max’s shared account does not establish that Max personally ran the commands. This excerpt identifies the abandoned probe without reproducing internal hosts or addresses.

detail.note: Selections from the diagnosis and the later cleanup. Option (a) was to remove the abandoned ingress; option (b) was to configure the child zone. The four records were the probe’s A and HTTPS records and two ownership TXT records. The shared historical account does not establish who wrote these comments, so they are attributed as work records. Commands, host addresses, and internal artifact locations are omitted.

selections.speaker: Work record
selections.text:
The Ingress routes to a Service named `dummy` that does not exist, in a namespace holding nothing
else. It has no ArgoCD tracking-id and no labels, and neither `tls-probe` nor `tls-test` appears
anywhere in `homelab-gitops/apps/` or `infrastructure/`. It was applied by hand on 2026-05-28 and
left behind.

[…]

That makes (a) strictly better than (b), and better than this issue assumed: deleting the Ingress
removes the cause, and it touches nothing in `apps/dnsweaver/configmap.yaml` — so **no ArgoCD sync
to production is involved**, which was the reason (b) was being held back. (b) would have been
building configuration to serve a dead probe.

selections.speaker: Work record
selections.text:
**Executed 2026-08-22 — option (a), the loop is stopped at the source.**

[…]

That is the zone-shadowing bug confirming itself: dnsweaver cannot read back the child zone it wrote into, so it cannot recognise its own record as an orphan. Both follow-up items in the description were therefore real, and all four records had to go by hand.

[…]

And dnsweaver's logs still show high volumes of `record already exists with correct target` at DEBUG across every hostname — that is normal idempotent behaviour and **not** this bug; the real symptom was Technitium rejecting the writes.

bookmark-intent.reference: Homepage conversation · the workflow Max wanted
bookmark-intent.excerpt: I want to make my browsers ephemeral and stop having 50 million tabs and tab groups.
bookmark-intent.context: Exact sentence from Max’s request. The number is his colloquial description, not a measured tab count. No browsing-history entries are included.

detail.note: Selected turns in their original order. Intervening messages are omitted; […] marks a cut within a message. This was the initial interpretation. The later bookmark passage follows the correction to the oversized result.

selections.speaker: Max
selections.text: I want to include all of the websites from every domain in here almost as a bookmark system. finance, government etc. all should be there. I want to make my browsers ephemeral and stop having 50 million tabs and tab groups.

selections.speaker: Codex
selections.text: Understood. I’ll revise this from a curated “frequent sites” tab into a durable browser-independent bookmark surface. I’ll keep the useful frequent tab, add every distinct destination domain—including finance and government—and exclude only hosts that are not usable destinations at all, such as tracking pixels or OAuth callback machinery.

bookmark-availability.context: An additional missing-configuration-file correction followed the catalogue work. The record reports a clean replacement pod and repeated successful page requests after MR !284. No current uptime claim is made from that historical check.

detail.note: Selected explanation of the missing configuration file and resulting availability gap. Hostnames, pod identifiers, and operational links are omitted.

selections.speaker: Codex
selections.text:
This was a real intermittent backend outage, not browser cache. The replacement pod restarted twice with exit code 1. Its previous log showed Homepage v1.13.2 failing to initialize `/app/config/proxmox.yaml`: it tried to copy the skeleton into `/app/config` and received `EACCES`. The operator ConfigMap/Deployment lacked both that key and its `subPath` mount; the household workload already had them.

[…]

The page currently returns 200 and the pod is Ready, but that is temporary rather than proof of stability until !284 is merged, reconciled, and observed without further restarts.

selections.speaker: Codex
selections.text:
Availability regression resolved and live-verified.

[…]

The live ConfigMap now supplies `proxmox.yaml: {}`, and the Deployment mounts it read-only at `/app/config/proxmox.yaml` using `subPath: proxmox.yaml`.

[…]

The browser screenshot was therefore a real transient single-backend gap caused by the previous pod exits, not stale browser content.

later-memories.reference: Returning to the search · later recollections
later-memories.excerpt: I remember more of all of this just by going through this process.
later-memories.context: In this September14 dictation, Max recalled the Mac box set, putting the discs into the drive, and a prebuilt little house in a 3D modeling program. These are later recollections, not facts the August search had independently proved.

detail.note: A longer selection from Max’s later dictation. The surrounding article-editing discussion is omitted.

selections.speaker: Max
selections.text: I since then have remembered that it was, in fact, the Mac box set. It was the seven discs or whatever. And I remember putting them into the disk drive and running the games because it was like two discs of games or one disc of games and then a bunch of other crap, right? selections.speaker: Work record
selections.text:
fix(journal-upload): survive a log-store restart instead of giving up forever

[…]

systemd-journal-upload EXITS when it cannot reach the store. The packaged unit
ships Restart=on-failure with StartLimitBurst=5 over the default 10s window, so
an unreachable store burns all five restarts within seconds and systemd then
gives up PERMANENTLY. The host silently stops shipping and nothing reports it.

[…]

Adds a drop-in with StartLimitIntervalSec=0 and Restart=always, RestartSec=30 -
retry forever with backoff rather than giving up. 30s is long enough not to
hammer a store that is still starting, short enough that an outage costs
seconds of buffered journal rather than minutes.

cold-model-record.context: Selected original text from the retained commit record. The timestamp is when the change was recorded; it does not establish when the work began or prove a live deployment.

detail.note: Selected commit text. […] marks omitted text. The timestamp records the change; it does not establish work duration or a live deployment.

selections.speaker: Work record
selections.text:
ai: let a cold Ollama model load finish, and stop unloading what took minutes to load

[…]

Restarting the Ollama pod for OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH threw away 83 days of page
cache, and that turned out to be the only reason model loads were ever fast.
Cold, qwen3.5:9b reaches progress 0.24 and hits Ollama's 5-minute default load
timeout; every retry restarts the clock, so it never finishes and every chat
turn 500s with 'unexpected server status: llm server loading model'.

[…]

A plain sequential read of the same volume measures 435 MB/s, so this is
Ollama's mmap access pattern against RBD rather than sick storage. Raise
OLLAMA_LOAD_TIMEOUT to 30m so a cold load completes, and set OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE
to 24h so a loaded model is not discarded after five idle minutes

fix(comfyui): stop the liveness probe killing the pod during model load

[…]

ComfyUI serves HTTP from the same thread that loads models, so it stops
answering for as long as a checkpoint takes to read - minutes for a ~7GB
safetensors coming cold off Ceph RBD. With the default timeoutSeconds: 1 and
failureThreshold: 3, kubelet concluded the container was wedged after 90
seconds of that and restarted it mid-generation, taking the queued work with

process is stuck, and readiness ~90 seconds before pulling it from the
service. Both keep their probes rather than dropping them, so a genuinely
hung process is still caught.

moments.title: A disc full of half-remembered games
moments.deck: One name survived. The others were a shovel, a tank, and insects on a screen.
paragraphs: Max came to the search with Chrysanthemum already in mind. He remembered a Macintosh magazine with games on a disc, or perhaps a pack of discs, and wanted to find what he had played. The other games were harder to name. There was a tank battle that might have been turn based, something like an old roguelike, and a Galaga-like game with insects.

Those descriptions were enough to begin a conversation, but they left room for a lot of wrong answers. Claude suggested candidates. Max supplied more details, including a shovel, sand, and places to visit, which moved the roguelike search toward TaskMaker. The useful clues came from that back and forth.

The disc mattered as much as any individual title. If they could find the collection, it might bring back games Max hadn't thought to ask about. His opening message also proposed a place on the website where some of them could be played. The search and the arcade started in the same idea.

time.note: A recorded moment; duration is unknown.

moments.quoteText: there was a tank battle thing, maybe turn based.

moments.title: Searching inside the discs
moments.deck: The archive descriptions could point to a collection. The file catalogs could say what was on it.
paragraphs: An archived CD can have a useful title and a description without telling you whether one particular application is buried inside it. The search had reached that limit. Claude proposed reading the old Macintosh file catalogs from the disc images themselves.

That changed the work. Instead of relying on a search result about a disc, the session could retrieve the portions containing its catalog and inspect the names stored there. Claude built the tools under Max's direction, using HTTP range requests to ask for pieces of an image. The early parser needed repairs before the results were useful.
A list of names was still only a beginning. The first promising Chrysanthemum result would make that clear. They needed to know where the file lived inside the collection.

time.note: A recorded moment; duration is unknown.

moments.quoteText: I can read the partition map and catalog extents over HTTP range requests

moments.title: The first names off the disc
moments.deck: Before the reader could find a game, it had to read the disc correctly.
paragraphs: The first attempt didn't produce a list of games. It reported that the image wasn't an HFS volume. The next attempt returned zero catalog bytes. Claude had proposed looking inside the discs, but the tool it was building couldn't yet do that reliably.

Claude inspected the volume information and corrected the reader. A few minutes later, the output contained recognizable software names. BBEdit and QuickDraw 3D were among them. They weren't the games Max was looking for, but they showed that the session could reach past the archive description and read names from the disc itself.
Later that evening, filenames beginning with Chrysanthemums would send the search into a collection of color palettes.

time.note: First and last selected records; this is elapsed time, not a measure of continuous work.

moments.title: Black and white, with some color mixed in
moments.deck: Max remembered black and white, and some color applications too.
paragraphs: Claude asked whether the Macintosh had been color or black and white, and whether Max could remember the magazine. Either answer might help narrow the collections being searched. Max remembered black and white, but he also remembered some color applications. He had been very young, and the machines, software, and magazines might have become mixed together in his memory.
The search still had to allow for more than one machine or collection.

time.note: A recorded moment; duration is unknown.

moments.title: The wrong flowers
moments.deck: The name matched. Its location told a different story.
paragraphs: Claude announced a hit on a MacAddict disc. The returned names looked close. They began with Chrysanthemums, followed by numbers. But close was not the same as the game Max remembered.

The session expanded the parser to recover complete paths. The promising entries were tucked inside a review of Chromatica, in a collection of palettes named after artists. These chrysanthemums belonged to Renoir.

The conversation kept the confident first announcement, the tool output, and the correction. Reading them together explains why the lead was abandoned. Repeating the announcement by itself would have preserved Claude's words accurately and still told the wrong story.

moments.title: The games missing from the list
moments.deck: A fuller listing lost names that the earlier search had already found.
paragraphs: By the early hours of August 19, Inside Mac Games had become a promising candidate. The search had found Swoop and TaskMaker on its October 1995 disc. But when Claude tried to recover the directory tree, those names were missing from the output.

The session now had two results from the same disc that didn't agree. Claude found that the tree reader was following only part of the catalog and changed it to inspect all of the nodes. The next output included the TaskMaker folder and paths for Swoop. The missing names had been a problem with the reader, rather than a reason to discard the disc.
Inside Mac Games stayed in consideration. It held several recognizable games, but this pass still had no Chrysanthemum match. The search continued with a better tool and an incomplete answer.

moments.title: The search was running, but going nowhere
moments.deck: An update request led back to the search machinery.
paragraphs: Max asked for an update. A search process was still running, but the file checks showed that part of the sweep had stopped producing new results. Claude traced the stall to archive entries that grouped thousands of individual disk images together. A worker was spending its time walking through those entries while the rest of the search appeared to wait.

Claude limited how much the sweep would take on from those entries and resumed it. The new output soon included MacCube Volume 1, with Chrysanthemum and Swoop together. That gave the conversation a different candidate to inspect.

The next step was to open the collection and see what else was there. The row in the search output wasn't enough to identify Max's childhood discs on its own, but it finally brought the name he remembered most clearly alongside another of the games.

moments.title: Several clues on the same discs
moments.deck: Several of the clues finally appeared together.
paragraphs: The search reached MacCube, a boxed shareware collection. Its first volume listed Chrysanthemum, Swoop, and a folder called Armor 1.1. TaskMaker appeared on another volume. Several of Max's clues now had a place beside one another.

moments.title: Save this. There are posts in it.
moments.deck: A new writing idea arrived before the search was finished.
paragraphs: Max's reply began with recognition and moved almost immediately to what they could do next. He saw more than the post about the games. The search itself could be another piece, and a browser arcade could give people something to try.

He asked for the detail to be kept so there would be material to return to. An idea had appeared while another project was in motion. Saving the detail gave it somewhere to wait until he had time to return.
The preserved conversation now supplies the clues, the failed lead, the change of method, and his reaction to the results. This companion returns to that record weeks later.

moments.title: Returning to a familiar collection
moments.deck: The candidate was waiting when Max came back to the conversation.
paragraphs: When he returned to the conversation that morning, he recognized the games. There was still a distinction between recognizing the software and identifying the exact discs he had owned. MacSilverWare also carried several of the same titles. The games had traveled through more than one collection.

Armor was the remaining tank-game candidate. It had a name now, and an application to investigate. In the same reply that welcomed the results, Max also started thinking about what else the search could become.

moments.title: Finding Armor
moments.deck: The application still had a way to explain itself.
paragraphs: A folder named Armor 1.1 was a lead, but the name alone did not tell Max whether it was his tank game. Claude had not found enough useful web information to identify it confidently. Claude could still inspect the application itself.

Classic Macintosh software could store help and credits in a resource fork, a separate part of the file. Claude wrote an extractor and retrieved Armor's resource fork from the MacSilverWare image. MacCube had supplied a promising listing; the extraction came from this other disc.

The retained material named Brad Sanders, carried a 1991 copyright notice, and described units moving and firing on a grid. The player commanded tanks and infantry. Movement and firing had separate phases. That gave the candidate a much more specific shape than the original memory of a battle that was perhaps turn based.

time.note: The retained extraction exchange. Max’s later confirmation is a separate moment.

moments.title: Only one game should be running
moments.deck: Trying the preview turned a collection of embeds into a player.
paragraphs: By the afternoon, there was a page for Max to try. He liked it and wanted more of the games available there, but he also wanted a way to keep them from running over one another. Adding another emulator for every game could leave several old computers competing inside one browser tab, with their sound and processor use piling up.

Max asked for the page to keep that under control. Claude rebuilt it around one active emulator. Starting a game would replace the one already running, and visiting the page would not start all of them in the background. The built HTML contained no emulator frames waiting to load automatically.
This was also where Max made the release pairing explicit. The arcade should go out with the post about the games.

moments.title: A clean build, and the wrong disc address
moments.deck: The page could compile while a game still pointed at a guess.
paragraphs: The rebuilt arcade passed its build, but Claude noticed two problems before calling the page ready. The address for MacCube Volume 2 had been guessed, and a page-load handler could attach the same controls twice. Neither mistake had stopped the site from compiling.

The archive metadata supplied the real disc filename. Claude replaced the guessed address and added a check to avoid binding a control that was already bound. After the patch, both mounted-disc addresses returned the requested chunks through the emulator proxy.
The corrected addresses could serve the disc data. Checking the games themselves would take more than a successful request.

time.note: First and last selected records; this is elapsed time, not a measure of continuous work.

moments.title: Could the games live here?
moments.deck: Finding them led to a place where someone else could play.
paragraphs: A first arcade preview existed before the disc-search conversation ended. Max wanted to see more of the games and emulate as many as possible. He also spotted a practical problem early. The emulators should not all keep running over one another.

His preference was to host the experience on his own systems, with care for the people who had made the software. That turned the project into more than a page of archival links. It needed game pages, media, emulator controls, and a way to start and stop a session without making the page fight itself.

moments.title: A DNS record that would not stay found
moments.deck: The proposed configuration fix was serving a test that no longer existed.
paragraphs: Elsewhere in the lab, DNSWeaver kept trying to recreate the same ownership record. The DNS server rejected each write because the record already existed. On the next cycle, the service tried again.

The investigation found a mismatch between where the DNS server placed a record and where DNSWeaver looked for it. Writes went into a more specific child zone; reads checked the configured parent zone. The record could exist without appearing in the next readback.

Adding configuration for the child zone was one possible answer. But the hostname belonged to an old test probe, and the investigation found that its ingress pointed to a service that did not exist. The test setup was still asking for DNS even though there was nothing left behind it. It did not need more configuration to keep it alive.

time.note: A dated part of the work. No duration is established by this record.

moments.quoteText: The Ingress routes to a Service named `dummy` that does not exist

moments.title: The old test could go
moments.deck: The later work record reports the cleanup and what remained unresolved.
paragraphs: The August 22 work record reports that the abandoned ingress was removed and the repeated-write loop stopped. The remaining records were then cleaned up manually. The underlying child-zone limitation remained a separate problem; stopping this loop had not fixed every case that could trigger it.

time.note: A dated part of the work. No duration is established by this record.

moments.quoteText: the loop is stopped at the source.

moments.title: The logs stopped coming
moments.deck: The store came back. Some of its senders did not.
paragraphs: A restart of the log store had left two machines no longer sending their logs. Their upload services had used up all of their restart attempts within seconds. When the store returned, those services stayed stopped.

The repair changed the retry behavior so an unavailable destination would lead to another attempt after a delay. It was ordinary maintenance, but the missing records mattered: a healthy log store could still be receiving an incomplete account of the lab.

time.note: Timestamp of the retained change record. Work duration is not established.

moments.title: Waiting for the model to load
moments.deck: A restart exposed how much the service had depended on cached data.
paragraphs: After a restart, the local model took long enough to load that the service gave up before it finished. Retrying meant starting over. The same model had seemed quick while its data was still cached.

The configuration change allowed a longer cold start and kept a loaded model available for longer. It also reduced the context allocation to leave room for the other model sharing the GPU. A setting that fit during an isolated test did not fit the ordinary workload.

time.note: Timestamp of the retained change record. Work duration is not established.

moments.title: Playback kept cutting out
moments.deck: A library scan was being interrupted by the service meant to keep playback healthy.
paragraphs: Max was watching something when Plex kept cutting out. The investigation recorded a metadata scan blocking the server long enough for its health check to restart it. That ended playback, and the scan resumed after the restart.
The committed fix gave the server more time before a failed liveness check would kill it.

time.note: Timestamp of the retained change record. Work duration is not established.

moments.title: Checking who was still sending
moments.deck: A total could look healthy while individual machines went quiet.
paragraphs: The earlier log-upload repair had addressed why the senders stopped. It had not provided a useful warning when a sender disappeared. Watching the total amount of incoming data could miss a small number of quiet machines.

The follow-up added a check for how many hosts were represented in recent logs. Its time window allowed for machines that naturally wrote very little. Otherwise, an ordinary quiet period could look like another failure.

time.note: Timestamp of the retained change record. Work duration is not established.

moments.title: Two jobs disappeared from the queue
moments.deck: The image tool was still loading when its health check decided it had stopped.
paragraphs: Two submitted image-generation jobs disappeared without producing output. The retained investigation tied the restart to a health check failing while the application loaded a large model.
The adjustment allowed a longer loading interval while retaining a way to detect a stuck process.

time.note: Timestamp of the retained change record. Work duration is not established.

moments.title: The last two red squares
moments.deck: The dashboard still needed work after the services were answering.
paragraphs: The new starting page still showed failures for services that could answer requests. One check used a hostname the recipe application would not accept. Others became unreliable when a whole page of checks ran together.
The change corrected the route for the recipe check and gave the slower checks more time.

time.note: Timestamp of the retained change record. Work duration is not established.

moments.title: The sentence had been cut short
moments.deck: Returning to the game uncovered a fault in the extraction tool.
paragraphs: Fact-checking the disc-search material brought the extraction tool back into use. Its import path still pointed to the place it had lived before moving into a repository. There was also a less obvious problem: the tool cut off printable strings after 120 characters.

That limit had left an incomplete sentence in the saved Armor notes. The repair made the imports relative to the tool and raised the extraction limit. The game had retained more of its instructions than the earlier capture showed.

time.note: Timestamp of the retained change record. Work duration is not established.

moments.title: Getting the recipes into the kitchen app
moments.deck: Nine recipes were already written down. They did not need typing out again.
paragraphs: The recipe collection already existed as Markdown in the notes vault. A small importer converted those entries into the structure Tandoor expected, avoiding a second round of typing them into forms.
The importer checked recipe names before adding entries. Running it again was meant to leave corrections made inside the kitchen app alone.

time.note: Timestamp of the retained change record. Work duration is not established.

moments.title: Reading the batteries
moments.deck: The backup power units needed to appear in the monitoring too.
paragraphs: The lab had two backup power units, but their battery readings were not being collected. This change added collectors for both, using the different interfaces each unit offered.
Collecting those readings was separate from deciding what should shut down during a power outage. The work record explicitly left automatic shutdown disabled.

time.note: Timestamp of the retained change record. Work duration is not established.

moments.title: Reading the site’s traffic
moments.deck: A small integration brought the analytics into the tools used around the lab.
paragraphs: Alongside the site itself, the work record adds an adapter for Umami, the site analytics service. That gave the AI tooling an integration for reading those analytics.

time.note: A dated part of the work. No duration is established by this record.

moments.title: A finished job was still in the alert
moments.deck: One monitoring rule needed to distinguish waiting from already done.
paragraphs: A later monitoring change excluded completed or failed pods from an alert about containers waiting to start. The rule needed to describe work that was still waiting, rather than continue reporting a job that had already reached its final state.

time.note: Timestamp of the retained change record. Work duration is not established.

moments.title: The test depended on the machine
moments.deck: An unreleased project needed a less fragile way to check its cache.
paragraphs: On another project, still unreleased, a test changed a font setting and expected the resulting files to differ. On a machine where both requested fonts resolved to the same fallback, that comparison could fail even when the application had refreshed its cached output correctly.
The revised test inspected the cache entries and generated content more directly.

time.note: Timestamp of the retained change record. Work duration is not established.

moments.title: A faster unpack, a larger download
moments.deck: Feedback on a private preview led back into the installer.
paragraphs: Installer walkthrough feedback on the same unreleased project led to a change in compression. The retained change describes a measured trade: a larger package, with less time spent unpacking it.
The private preview was also getting adjustments to its controls and visual presentation.

time.note: Timestamp of the retained change record. Work duration is not established.

moments.title: The browser could do the old computer’s work
moments.deck: The next selected arcade record describes how it would run.
paragraphs: By September 7, the preparation record described the chosen division of work. The cluster served the files; the visitor's browser ran the emulation and kept the saves. There was no separate server-side machine for each player. The browser was doing the old computer's work.
Getting that arrangement to run in a test environment was one step. The next check had to follow the route a visitor would actually take.

time.note: A dated part of the work. No duration is established by this record.

moments.quoteText: emulation and saves run in the browser, while the cluster serves immutable files.

moments.title: It worked until it went the long way around
moments.deck: A visitor's route exposed a problem the origin checks had missed.
paragraphs: The arcade could load games at its origin. The release checks had reached actual play, not just a healthy web page. Then the checks followed the public route through Cloudflare, where the emulators' requests for disk blocks encountered a rate limit.

That changed the meaning of the earlier success. The files and emulators could work while the route in front of them still prevented a visitor from getting far enough to play. The September 7 comment recorded the failure instead of calling the external release verified.
A later report recorded the scoped correction and another run through the public route. Windows 95 booted, and GTA 2 reached the city and accepted movement.

moments.title: The games had a story around them
moments.deck: The arcade could show what Max played. The memoir could say what it meant to him.
paragraphs: The disc hunt supplied names and files, but it could not write Max's memories for him. He wanted to write the personal piece himself. The manuscript followed the games into the larger story of how he got into computers, with the recovery of those old titles bringing the account back to the present.

The arcade was released on September 7. The memoir followed on September 8, with links between the writing and the playable collection. The post's research-assist label and process note explained where AI had helped with finding the games and editing the supplied prose.
The memoir remains Max's account of his life. The arcade gives its readers a way to spend some time with the games themselves.

moments.title: A starting page for the household
moments.deck: The shared page and the administration page could serve different purposes.
paragraphs: The dashboard work separated a shared household starting page from the page used to operate the lab. The preparation included a catalogue of household destinations and desktop and mobile examples.
It was another use for a starting page: somewhere to open the services used around the house, without starting from an administrator’s collection of tools.

time.note: A dated part of the work. No duration is established by this record.

moments.title: The backup needed somewhere to write
moments.deck: It failed before it could reach the backup repository.
paragraphs: An attended backup of the household inventory service reached Restic and then failed. The program had chosen a cache location on its read-only root filesystem.
The fix pointed that cache at an existing temporary volume where it could write. A read-only check could then inspect the repository, which contained no snapshots yet.

time.note: A dated part of the work. No duration is established by this record.

moments.title: The browser was not supposed to be storage
moments.deck: Saving useful destinations meant understanding which parts of the browsing record mattered.
paragraphs: Max wanted to be able to discard a browser session without losing the useful things he had found. Keeping more tabs and tab groups was becoming its own kind of storage. A searchable starting page could hold the destinations while the browser itself stayed temporary.

The request grew from frequently visited sites into a broader bookmark system. Max clarified that finance, government, and other ordinary parts of his life belonged there too. The next implementation took that breadth literally and produced one card for every host in the supplied export.

time.note: A dated part of the work. No duration is established by this record.

moments.quoteText: I want to make my browsers ephemeral and stop having 50 million tabs and tab groups.

moments.title: Every host was too much
moments.deck: The first catalogue had taken the request too literally.
paragraphs: He reviewed the result and sent it back. A browser history contains more than places someone would deliberately bookmark. It also contains authentication handoffs, duplicate service hosts, temporary previews, and incidental stops. Keeping the categories he used did not mean keeping every piece of infrastructure the browser had passed through.
The correction reduced the archive of 881 hosts to 38 selected destinations. The work record ties that change to MR !283.

time.note: The recorded correction and delivery in this episode. A subsequent availability repair is shown separately.

moments.title: The new starting page needed one more fix
moments.deck: A missing configuration file interrupted the corrected page.
paragraphs: A separate availability repair followed the catalogue change. A missing configuration file had caused the application to restart. The later work record reports a clean replacement and repeated successful page requests after MR !284.
The goal was a place he could return to, without requiring the browser session to remember everything for him.

time.note: A dated part of the work. No duration is established by this record.

moments.title: Waiting for the last change
moments.deck: The preview test was replying before the final request had been sent.
paragraphs: A week later, a test on the unreleased project was exercising a preview while settings changed. It could select a request that was newer than the original one but still older than the change waiting to be sent.
The correction used the test clock to finish that short delay before choosing the reply. The test could then respond to the latest settings request.

time.note: Timestamp of the retained change record. Work duration is not established.

moments.title: Returning to the conversation
moments.deck: The detail saved for later became the material for this timeline.
paragraphs: In September, Max returned to the game search while thinking about his next post. The retained conversation gave him more than the answer to a forgotten title. It showed the questions he had asked, the directions Claude had tried, the correction after the false hit, and the point where he recognized Armor.

Returning to the search also brought more memories back. By September 14, Max recalled putting the discs from the Mac box set into the drive and could picture a little house from a 3D modeling program. More of the collection was coming back to him than the games he had originally been able to name.

He wanted that material to read as a story. The sources could sit underneath it for anyone who wanted to look more closely, without requiring everyone to reconstruct the sequence from a list of issues and comments.

The interface followed the same idea. A timeline could show the larger work, then make room for a chapter. Max chose a vertical version that could be scrolled through, with explicit controls for looking closer. He also wanted several threads to explore, including the tangents that appeared while something else was underway.
The August request to save the detail is one of those connections. It gives this return somewhere concrete to begin.
